en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha, in one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Jeta Grove, in the Anāthapiṇḍada Park, at Śrāvastī.
At the Kūṭāgāraśālā, he was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus and five hundred bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were well-known to the public.

At that time, the World-Honored One was residing in the great city of Śrāvastī. Then the king, ministers, brahmins, householders, and their retinues made offerings, paid homage, showed respect, and offered praise to him, providing many offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine.

He is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, the Sugata, the Lokavid, the Anuttara, the Puruṣadamyasārathi, the Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Buddha, the Bhagavat. He is accomplished in his place of birth and accomplished in his lineage; he is endowed with samādhi, endowed with wisdom, endowed with liberation, and endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation. He is endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. He proclaims the sublime Dharma, which is good in the beginning, middle, and end, with beautiful words and meanings, complete with the pure and stainless holy life. He is endowed with the five eyes—namely, the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Buddha eye, and the Dharma eye—and he thoroughly knows the abodes of this world and other worlds.
At that time, the World-Honored One had successfully subdued the non-Buddhist Nirgrantha Jñātiputra and others; the Buddha-dharma flourished, and he was revered by devas and humans alike.
When the time arrived, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and, surrounded by a retinue of bhikṣus, entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.

In his coming and going, advancing and halting, his majestic deportment was composed and orderly; his gaze was serene and his movements—bending, stretching, bowing, and rising—as well as his grasping of the robe and bowl, were all perfectly dignified. His golden, wondrous body radiated brilliance, like a mass of fierce fire, a precious gem, or the sun and moon illuminating the dark night. Adorned with the thirty-two marks, he stepped upon the threshold of the gate with his golden feet.
At that time, the great city of Śrāvastī manifested various unprecedented wonders, as described in these verses:
"When the Sage of Men enters, The Lion of the Śākyas treads upon the threshold;
He manifests many rare and marvelous events— Listen with a pure mind as I speak."
The blind gained sight to see; the deaf gained the power to hear;
the naked received clothing; and those who were deranged regained right mindfulness.
All rejoiced with palms joined, gazing upon the Buddha without ever being satiated.
The various drums resounded spontaneously, and flutes and pipes produced sounds of their own accord.
Geese, quails, doves, and mandarin ducks all emitted wondrous and gentle notes.
Those who had lost their wealth found treasuries of jewels, and the various precious objects themselves gave forth sound.
At that time, the earth shook in six ways, and those who lacked faith attained a pure mind.
As the Supreme Awakened One lowered his feet to step forth, pure lotus flowers received him;
touching sentient beings with peace and bliss, they were reborn in heaven upon the end of their lives.
The woman suffers in her pregnancy, yet gives birth to a wondrous son in peace and joy;
free from the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion, it is so for both parents and the child alike.
The steps and stairways are exquisitely adorned, and many billions of devas rain down flowers.
Sentient beings were free from illness, And liberated from all suffering.
When the Sugata entered the city, All experienced peace and happiness;
Each thought, "I have offered him food," And each thought, "The Buddha is looking at me."
"The merit and power of this human seer cannot be fully described by me.

At that time, the World-Honored One was walking for alms in succession through the great city of Śrāvastī. When he reached a certain spot along the way, there was a deserted place where an infant had been abandoned—one of handsome appearance and exceedingly fair complexion, sucking its own right finger. In that deserted place were many foxes, wolves, and dogs; yet upon seeing the infant, they merely licked it and departed, none being able to harass or harm it.
This infant is a person of merit who has long planted roots of goodness.

Many people dwell upon observing him and give rise to a sense of wonder; they come and go, gazing at this child abandoned in a desolate place, who is so upright, dignified, and lovely that they joyfully delight in beholding him.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing a great multitude of people coming and going through the open space, though he already knew the reason, asked intentionally, addressing Ānanda:
"You should go there and observe what these people are doing as they come and go through the open space."
Ānanda replied, “So it is, World-Honored One!”

The Venerable Ānanda immediately went to an open space and saw that the infant was of handsome and dignified appearance; he was sucking his own right finger and gazing intently at the multitude with unblinking eyes.
Having seen this, Ānanda returned to the Buddha’s presence and reported exactly what he had seen:
"World-Honored One!
In this secluded place there is an abandoned infant, whose countenance is so upright and majestic that it is most worthy of veneration, like a precious image."
He gazed at the people with unblinking eyes.

At that time, the World-Honored One gave rise to a heart of compassion for the infant; observing his original roots of goodness, he knew they had reached maturity and were capable of understanding the meaning of the Dharma he was about to teach. Furthermore, knowing that the roots of goodness of sentient beings had matured, he immediately went to where the infant was.
Having arrived, he stood to one side and addressed the infant with these verses:
"The evil karma created in the past, Its retribution now appears here.
Abandoned in this desolate place, The infant suffers thus."
At that time, the infant, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power and his own innate roots of goodness, replied to the Buddha in verse:
"Gautama, you still possess the perception of an abandoned empty place;
when you were at the site of enlightenment, did you not know this perception?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"I have already known all perceptions, yet I am forever without perception;
out of compassion for you, I have come to this empty place."
At that time, the infant spoke again in verse:
"If sentient beings cannot be found, And ultimately cannot be apprehended;
for whom, O Honored One, do you feel compassion?"
"By whom is this compassionate mind stirred?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Sentient beings do not know this: That there is no self, and that all is empty and quiescent."
"In order to awaken them, I travel through villages and towns.
At that time, the infant spoke again in verse:
"Thoroughly understanding emptiness and quiescence, awakening to emptiness and quiescence;"
"Does the Tathāgata still possess the notion of a sentient being, such that he does not sever it?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The Buddha’s power of compassion is thus; having realized emptiness and quiescence,"
"To transform and guide sentient beings, the Teacher expounds the Dharma.
At that time, the infant spoke again in verse:
"Are there still inversions remaining? Has the Tathāgata not yet severed them?"
"Without the perception of sentient beings being born, can one thus give rise to compassion?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Sustained by the Buddha’s protection, the Bodhisattva generates diligence."
"For the sake of sentient beings who do not understand, the Honored One among Men has manifested this adornment.
At that time, the infant spoke again in verse:
"This is the adornment of delusion;"
"If one does not perceive objects, and if dharmas are not such objects, by what means could adornment arise?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"This power of great compassion tames and guides the world in this manner."
"Remaining unattached to things, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
At that time, the infant spoke again in verse:
"The Dharma has no words or letters; how can it be expounded?"
"The world suffers a great defeat, Teaching what is not Dharma as Dharma.
Then the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"I do not bring ruin to the world; I do not speak what is not Dharma."
“Sentient beings are themselves deluded and inverted; I shall liberate them from their fetters.
At that time, the infant spoke again in verse:
“The fetters and afflictions have no root, nor do they have any location.”
"Furthermore, it does not exist within or without; from what could one be liberated from those fetters?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Arising from false conceptualization, it coexists with inversion."
"To sever those delusive thoughts, O infant,
I shall preach the Dharma.
At that time, the infant spoke again in verse:
“The nature of the mind is eternally pure; within it there are no defilements or fetters.
Even if there are many discursive thoughts, the pure nature does not give rise to defilement.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Just as you have said, the nature of the mind is inherently and eternally pure;
it is only through adventitious afflictions and the dust of fetters that those lacking wisdom give rise to defilement.
At that time, the infant spoke again in verse:
“Knots have no location, nor can they be found in any direction;
how then can they be said to arise?
I pray that you will explain this for me.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Just as clouds in the sky, Are visible yet lack reality;
So too do the fetters arise— Though seen, they possess no substance."
At that time, the infant spoke again in verse:
“The Dharma is equal to suchness (tathatā), and its very nature of arising is suchness;
if the Dharma were a true reality, suchness would be unattainable.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"All things are not as they appear; They abide equally within suchness (*tathatā*).
Having awakened to this suchness, There is neither fault nor merit."
At that time, the infant spoke again in verse:
"If no sentient beings are found, O Gautama! With whom could there be a combination?"
First observe the fundamental nature of phenomena: from whom do afflictions arise?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“In the past and the future, as well as in the present world,”
"The Buddha knows and perceives clearly, preaching the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
At that time, the infant spoke another verse:
"Regarding what is expounded as the three periods of time, and saying 'I am able to know it'—"
"This would constitute great arrogance, and it would be a case of self-exaltation.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"I do not exalt myself, nor do I disparage others."
"Manifesting as suchness and so forth, for this reason he is called the Tathāgata.
At that time, the infant spoke again in verse:
"Since nothing can be apprehended, it is not associated with verbal expression;"
"It is not that words are used to express speech; this 'is' is not like 'is.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Ordinary people follow after perceptions; within suchness, they give rise to false conceptions."
"To sever the notion of a self, the Tathāgata has appeared in the world.
At that time, the infant spoke another verse:
"There is no appearance in the world of Perfect Enlightenment, for it is well-cultivated as non-arising."
"Within the dharma of non-arising, the Buddha’s emergence is incongruous.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"Though non-arising, there is manifest arising; the appearance of the Buddha in the world is a manifestation."
"This is an explanation according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), not according to the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
At that time, the infant spoke again in verse:
"There still remain two conceptions: conventional truth and the ultimate truth."
"Within the path of the Single Vehicle, Gautama, you preach what is contradictory.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"I do not preach what is contradictory; I abide in non-contradiction."
They act for the sake of sentient beings who are in opposition;
O infant, know it thus!
At that time, the infant spoke again in verse:
"I repent for what I have said above before the Perfectly Awakened One;
It is by the power of the Buddha’s sustaining grace That I am able to speak thus."
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his golden arm from within his robe and raised the infant.
Thereupon, the infant grasped the Buddha’s finger and rose from the ground.
At that time, the World-Honored One took the infant from that empty place and proceeded toward the main thoroughfare.
Then the great assembly experienced what they had never known before; they redoubled their reverent salutations toward the World-Honored One and exclaimed:
"How extraordinary!"
“The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, having attained such sublime and wondrous dharmas, is now able to cause this one who is in extreme suffering and distress to dwell securely in these dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the infant, saying:

“Your karmic actions are exhausted; you should call to mind the roots of goodness you originally cultivated—causing this great assembly to give rise to a sense of rare wonder—and manifest great supernormal powers.”

At that time, the infant ascended into the air to the height of seven tala trees; from his body he emitted a radiance, and this light shone everywhere throughout the trichiliocosm, the world-system of the Buddha.

By means of this light, Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, and hundreds of thousands of other devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, having seen this light, came to the place where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and scattered various celestial flowers as an offering to the Buddha.
Having made this offering, he addressed the World-Honored One in these words:
“The radiance of the Bodhisattva is inconceivable; from his body he emits light that universally illuminates this Buddha-world, enabling immeasurable sentient beings to attain inconceivable benefit.”
"This child shall be named Acintyaprabha.
Then the World-Honored One Śākyamuni approved this name, saying:
"This child shall indeed be named Acintyaprabha."

At that time, the infant Acintyaprabha descended from the sky and, having stood upon the ground, through the Buddha’s spiritual power and the force of his own roots of goodness, his form became like that of an eight-year-old boy.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra immediately offered a celestial robe to the infant and spoke to him, saying: "Infant!
Out of compassion for us, please accept this celestial robe and do not remain naked."
At that time, the infant Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
“Kauśika! A bodhisattva does not regard fine garments as sublime; rather, he should wear the dharma-robes as his true adornment.”
Kauśika! Listen well now to that which is the medicine taken by a bodhisattva. Kauśika!
The bodhicitta is the robe of a bodhisattva, which leads to the fulfillment at the site of enlightenment and the complete perfection of all Buddha-dharmas.
Having a sense of shame and a dread of blame is the robe of a bodhisattva, by which they tame and bring all sentient beings to maturity, establishing them in faultlessness.
The adornment of firm vows is the robe of a bodhisattva, for the sake of accomplishing all tasks.
Integrity and freedom from deceit are the robe of a bodhisattva, for the sake of achieving the eradication of illusions, delusions, and falsehoods.
Diligent and ardent exertion is the robe of a bodhisattva, because it brings to fulfillment and completion all roots of goodness.
Aspiration, desire, and joy are the robe of a bodhisattva, because they bring to fulfillment all the Buddha-dharmas.
Abandoning pride is the robe of a bodhisattva, because it brings to fulfillment all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
Seeking the Dharma and hearing the Dharma is the robe of a bodhisattva, because it brings to fulfillment the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
Not giving rise to pride regarding wisdom is the robe of a bodhisattva, because it brings to fulfillment and completion the wisdom that is free from attachment.
Bringing about benefit is the robe of a bodhisattva, because it possesses compassionate awareness for all sentient beings.
Relinquishing all things is the robe of a bodhisattva, because it brings to fulfillment the perfection of the primary and secondary marks.
Guarding and upholding pure precepts is the robe of a bodhisattva, because it brings vows to fulfillment.
Harmonious patience is the robe of a bodhisattva, because it brings to ultimate fulfillment the sound of the Brahma-voice.
Firm and vigorous diligence, free from a mind of indolence or retreat, is the robe of a bodhisattva, because it brings to fulfillment the transcendence of all things.
Attaining all dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis is the robe of a bodhisattva, because it brings to fulfillment the great pervasive wisdom.
Indestructible wisdom is the robe of a bodhisattva, because it achieves the severance of all fetters, views, and hindrances.
The wisdom of great skillful means is the robe of a bodhisattva, for it accomplishes the teaching and transformation of all sentient beings.
Great compassion is the robe of a bodhisattva, for it accomplishes the rescue and protection of all sentient beings.
Great compassion is the robe of a bodhisattva, for it brings about the fulfillment of being free from weariness amidst birth and death.
Great joy is the robe of a bodhisattva, for it brings about the fulfillment of being endowed with the joy of the Dharma.
Great equanimity is the robe of a bodhisattva, for it brings about the abandonment of thoughts of attachment and aversion.
Having no intent to harm sentient beings is the robe of a bodhisattva, for it achieves non-affliction toward both oneself and others.
Expounding and preaching the Dharma is the robe of a bodhisattva, for it accomplishes the non-exaltation of oneself and the non-deprecation of others.
Practicing according to the teaching is the robe of a bodhisattva, for it accomplishes the severance of all fetters and latent tendencies.
"Kauśika! You should know that the Dharma-robe of a bodhisattva is thus adorned with the Dharma, so that one is never born naked.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra increased his reverence, affection, and respect for the infant, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Out of compassion for us, please let this infant accept these robes.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the infant Bodhisattva Inconceivable Light:
“Accept the robes of Śakra.”
Then the World-Honored One took the robe with his right hand and bestowed it upon the infant.
At that time, the infant knelt with his right knee on the ground, received the robe with his right hand, and having received it, immediately put it on.
At that time, the World-Honored One, taking the infant Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha, went through the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms in succession.

At that moment, the great assembly—men and women, old and young, elders and lay devotees, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, kings, and their ministers—upon seeing the infant Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha, gave rise to a sense of rare wonder; they also gathered together, all coming to pay homage and make offerings to the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One went on his almsround in due order and arrived at the house of the mother who had given birth to the Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha.
Then the Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha entered the house, approached his mother, and addressed her in verse:
"Mother, you have committed no fault; You ought to rejoice within yourself."
This is due to my own past evil karma, that I am now dwelling within my mother’s womb.
My mother is my field of merit; out of compassion for her who gave me birth, may she not feel ashamed, but go quickly to where the Tathāgata dwells.
"The mother has now attained great benefit because she carries me in her womb;
regarding such merit as this, go and inquire of the Teacher.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha said to Śakra-devānām-indra:
“Kauśika! Give me the incense, flowers, robes, and other necessities required; I wish to present them to my mother.
My mother shall use these to make offerings to the Buddha and shall resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra presented the Bodhisattva with celestial māndārava flowers, celestial incense, and various celestial garments.
Then, the Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha addressed his mother in verse:
"Accepting these pleasing flowers— divine and wondrous *mandārava* blossoms,
exquisite perfumes, and garments— to offer them up to the Sage of the Śākyas;
neither food, drink, nor jewels can repay the kindness of one's parents."
To guide them toward the True Dharma is to make offerings to one's two parents.
Having made offerings to the Honored One among bipeds, one should give rise to the pure mind of the supreme path;
I have constantly exhorted them throughout the long night, repeatedly and diligently at all times.
Her mother gave rise to a heart of joy and felt no shame at all;
she went to the presence of the Sage among Men, and having paid her respects, stood before him.
She scattered flowers upon the Tathāgata and offered both flowers and robes.
The roots of goodness planted by the Buddha immediately gave rise to the bodhicitta.
Firmly abiding in that bodhicitta, she questioned the Lion of the Śākyas:
"I am pregnant with a pure being; I pray you, speak of the karmic reward for this merit."
“By virtue of this wholesome karma, you shall not be born into the various miserable realms;
having made offerings to many billions of Buddhas, you shall attain Buddhahood.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished his almsround by sequential begging in the great city of Śrāvastī, departed from the great city of Rājagṛha together with the Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha and the great assembly, heading toward the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery.
When the World-Honored One had finished eating, he rinsed his mouth and hands, rose from his seat, and sat down again to expound the True Dharma.

At that time, King Prasenajit of the kingdom of Kośala heard that the infant Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha possessed great and inconceivable supernatural powers. Having heard this, he arrayed his fourfold army and proceeded toward the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery, to visit the World-Honored One.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
King Prasenajit addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Venerable World-Honored One!
“Where is the infant Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha?
We have heard that he possesses such inconceivable power of supernatural transformations.
At that time, the Buddha immediately showed King Prasenajit the infant Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha.

At that time, the king beheld this infant, the Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha, whose form and color were so upright and majestic as to surpass those of the gods; he was free from all fear and was adorned with the precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Having seen this, he then thought:
"By planting what roots of goodness and by accumulating what merit has such a wondrous body come to be?
At that time, the infant Acintyaprabha, empowered by the Buddha's spiritual authority, knew the thoughts in the mind of the King of Kośala and addressed the Great King with these verses:
"Constantly cultivating a mind of loving-kindness to purify sentient beings, Free from coarseness and impurity while practicing right mindfulness,
Restraining body, speech, and mind to purify the holy life— Such a one possesses this pure and wondrous body."
Those who distance themselves from evil and do not commit it themselves, Who increase, cultivate, and accumulate immeasurable goodness,
And abandon all strife and contention— Such persons possess a pure and wondrous body.
Revering the Buddha, the Dharma, and the noble Saṅgha, Constantly offering various sublime gifts,
Not reviling or insulting others nor causing them distress— Such is the pure and wondrous body they possess.
Toward others, they do not give rise to such things as teasing, scolding, or disparagement;
they speak only of praise and excellence, never of faults. Such is their pure and wondrous body.
"Avoiding stinginess, greed, envy, and pride, one observes one's own conduct and does not disparage others;
such a person possesses this pure and wondrous body.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"This infant, the Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha, has accomplished such a sublime and wondrous Great Dharma;
what karmic obstruction could have caused him to be born from the womb of this courtesan and then abandoned in a desolate place?"
The Buddha told the Great King:

"In the past, ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin who appeared in the world—a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. Great King, you should know that at that time, within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, there were two bodhisattvas:
one named Bhadradatta and the other named Dhanapati."

The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla had attained non-retrogression in the unsurpassed path; he had acquired dhāraṇīs and unimpeded eloquence, realized the patience of the non-arising of phenomena, possessed the majestic power of merit, maintained few desires and few affairs, constantly delighted in solitary dwelling, and had attained supernormal powers.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bahudhana practiced the dhūta austerities and served as an attendant to the Bodhisattva Bhadradatta.
That man constantly traveled to villages and cities, having many affairs to attend to.
The Bodhisattva Bhadradatta rebuked and instructed him, saying:
"For what reason do you engage in so many worldly affairs instead of abandoning them?
Though he admonished him repeatedly, the other became angry and felt resentment in his heart.
Because of his anger and resentment, he ruins his own body and mind; having ruined his body and mind, he speaks with malice and insults, saying:
"You are a lowly daughter born of illicit intercourse, obtained from another man."
"He does not even know his father, nor does he know his mother; how much less could you possibly possess morality, learning, concentration, or wisdom?
Having thus reviled him with anger, he neither repented nor desisted; bound by the fetters of affliction, he remained constantly possessed of a mind of resentment toward the Bodhisattva Bhadrottara.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadradatta immediately abandoned her.

Having abandoned her, he became even more enraged, reviling and slandering her while proclaiming her faults. Due to the causal conditions of these unwholesome karmic actions, when his body perished and his life ended, he was reborn in the womb of a courtesan—yet because he had been protected by the Bodhisattva Bhadradatta, he did not fall into hell. Once born, the courtesan constantly cast him away, so that he was devoured by foxes, wolves, and dogs.
"Great King! For this reason, throughout ninety-one kalpas, she has always died in this manner; in every birth she has been abandoned and reviled by the multitudes, who called her:
'This is a lewd woman.'"
"Cast away into a desolate place, he was devoured by foxes, wolves, and dogs.
Your Majesty, do not doubt this. Why is that?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Abhīru-dhana, who reviled him with anger, was none other than this present Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha.

Having exhausted his evil karma through the power of his wholesome deeds, he purified his mind of fetters and pleased the Buddha’s mind; thus, for this person, the miserable realms have been forever extinguished.
"Great King!

This Bodhisattva Inconceivable Light has already encountered sixty-four billion Buddhas, whom he has reverently served, made offerings to, honored, and praised; under these Buddhas, he has constantly practiced the pure life and diligently sought the Dharma."
This is the power of one's original roots of goodness, by which such matters and supernormal powers are attained.
Great King!

Thus, black and white karmic actions never perish; for this reason, the wise carefully guard their physical, verbal, and mental actions, preferring to sacrifice their own bodies and lives rather than committing evil deeds.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Has that Bodhisattva Bhadradatta already attained all-knowledge?"
"Is it for this reason that you cultivate and accumulate the bodhisattva practices?
The Buddha said, "Great King!"
"That Bodhisattva Bhadradatta is now practicing the bodhisattva path in that land of Akṣobhya Buddha; his name is Guṇakośa.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
If good sons or good daughters always should associate with spiritual friends and stay close to spiritual friends. Why is this?
World-Honored One!

Associating with virtuous friends, one reverently surrounds them to hear the sublime Dharma; having heard the sublime Dharma, one attains a virtuous mind; possessing a virtuous mind, one then cultivates virtuous conduct and performs wholesome deeds, tending toward favorable rebirths and thereby gaining virtuous friends.
Because one has gained such virtuous friends, one refrains from all evils and practices all forms of goodness.
Having practiced these virtues, one is personally free from distress and does not cause distress to others.
"If there is a bodhisattva who protects themselves and protects others, they will be able to attain bodhi;
if they have already established themselves in the Way, they possess great power and are able to bring benefit to others.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, Great King! You have spoken these words most aptly. Great King!
“A bodhisattva who draws near to spiritual friends will fulfill all meritorious qualities and wholesome dharmas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Inconceivable Light addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“By accomplishing how many dharmas does a bodhisattva swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and obtain the pure dharma-patience?
The Buddha said, “Infant!”
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will swiftly attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path as well as the pure dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*).
What are these four? They are:

understanding the patience of dependent origination and remaining far removed from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism; understanding that there is no self, person, sentient being, or life-span; and understanding emptiness and stillness while practicing within emptiness.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas.
What are these four?
The past is quiescent; the future is known to have no coming; the present does not abide; and the three periods of time are equal. These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely: self-purification, purifying all sentient beings, purifying the Dharma, and purifying meditative concentration.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas: namely, tranquility of body, tranquility of mind, tranquility of the path, and tranquility of the Dharma;
these are the four.

“Furthermore, there are four dharmas: namely, to contemplate the Buddha through the Dharma rather than through form; to contemplate the Dharma through detachment rather than through a self; to contemplate the Saṃgha through the unconditioned rather than through a multitude; and to purify the eye of wisdom. These are the four.”

“Furthermore, there are four dharmas: namely, fulfilling all the pāramitās; not abandoning the four means of integration (saṃgrahavastu); skillfully knowing expedient means (upāya); and preaching that there are no sentient beings while practicing great compassion (mahākaruṇā).
These are the four.”
“Infant! These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva accomplishes the swift attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and profound dharma-patience.

When this teaching was spoken, the Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); filled with joy and exultation, he ascended into the air to a height of seven tala trees.

At that time, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways; a great light shone everywhere, the heavens rained down various flowers, and hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having known the mind of the Bodhisattva Inconceivable Light, immediately smiled.
It is the constant law of the Buddhas that when they smile, various hundreds of thousands of colors of light—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and crystal—issue forth from the gateway of their face.

This light shone universally, pervading immeasurable and boundless worlds; it eclipsed the palaces of Māra as well as the sun and moon, and having severed the sufferings of the hells and the hungry ghosts, it ascended as far as the Brahma world, then returned to circumambulate the Buddha three times before entering through the mark of the uṣṇīṣa on his crown.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke this verse to ask him:
“Your physical marks are most subtle and wondrous; Your body is adorned with various excellences.
With your halo, you skillfully answer all questions; For what cause and condition do you smile?”
With supreme conduct of precepts and fearlessness, adorned with sublime concentration and wisdom, you manifest the fruit of steadfast liberation; for what cause and condition do you smile?
With the power of patience and the ten powers, patient and courageous, you are unshakable.
You who delight in showing the Four Noble Truths, for what cause and condition do you smile?
Your vajra-body is firm and solid, possessing the full strength of Nārāyaṇa;
your Brahma-voice is pleasing to the mind—pray, expound the meaning of your smile.
The Brahmakāyika devas above cannot see the crown of the Tathāgata’s head;
they join their palms in successive reverence. For what cause and condition do you smile?
Having descended from the King of Trees to subdue Māra, you have attained the stainless, pure path.
Knowing the conduct of all sentient beings, may you reveal for what reason you smile.
You turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma and preach impermanence, shaking the earth;
you discipline humans, devas, nāgas, and others—O Great Virtuous One, why do you smile?
“Illuminating and dispelling the darkness, With stainless and all-pervading pure eyes, Your merit is like space; For what cause and condition do you smile?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Do you now see this Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha, who stands seven *tāla* trees above the ground,
dwelling in the void? Ānanda replied,
"I have seen him."
“World-Honored One!

“Ānanda! This Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha shall, after the passing of hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, attain Buddhahood; he shall also be named Acintyaprabha—appearing in the world as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His land shall be named Viśuddha, and his kalpa shall be named Anavadya.”
Ānanda! This pure buddha-field is exceedingly pure, like the palaces of the devas in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations.
That Buddha’s lifespan will be twenty intermediate kalpas; his great assembly of śrāvakas will number eighty thousand, and the saṅgha of bodhisattvas will number thirty-two thousand.
Ānanda! For what reason is the eon named "Faultless"? Ānanda!

At that time, for many hundreds of thousands of kalpas no Buddha had appeared in the world; thus, this Buddha Inconceivable Light was the very first to attain Buddhahood within those kalpas. The gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens rejoiced and praised him, saying:
"This kalpa is free from fault! This kalpa is free from fault!"
"Because a Tathāgata has appeared in the world, this kalpa shall therefore be named 'Faultless'.
When the Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha spoke these words, thirty-two thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
and sixty thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Five hundred bhikṣus severed all fetters and outflows, attained mastery over their minds, and became arhats.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:

"Receive this sūtra; uphold, read, recite, and explain it. Proclaim it extensively among the great assembly so that my True Dharma may long abide in the world, and so that it may bring great benefit to future bodhisattvas."
The Venerable Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One,
I have received and upheld it.”
World-Honored One!
What is the name of this sutra?
How should it be upheld?
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!

This sutra is named ‘Eliminating the Obstructions of Karma through Purity,’ and it is also named ‘That Which Is Sustained by Spiritual Power and Spoken by the Bodhisattva Inconceivable Light. You should uphold it thus.”

Ānanda! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, for the duration of their entire lifespan, were to serve the Tathāgatas, making offerings, honoring, respecting, and praising them—with various colored flowers filling a basket as large as Mount Sumeru, and likewise with incense, powdered incense, ointment incense, banners, flags, and precious parasols—using these to make offerings;

Furthermore, if there are sons or daughters of good family who receive and uphold this sūtra taught by the Inconceivable Light, reciting it until they have mastered it, and extensively expound it for others among the great assembly while practicing according to its teachings, their merit shall be far greater than that.
Ānanda! If you wish to make a Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata, and if you wish to produce the radiance of great wisdom, you should receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Bodhisattva Inconceivable Light, the Venerable Ānanda, and the entire great assembly—including humans, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and others—having heard what the Buddha taught, were all filled with great joy.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha (Inconceivable Light)
